UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                        BEFORE THE
                          FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Avista Corp.                                        )                         Docket No. ER26-2793
PacifiCorp                                          )                         Docket No. ER26-2795
Northwestern Corp.                                  )                         Docket No. ER26-2802
Portland General Electric Company                   )                         Docket No. ER26-2809

                           MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND
                       ANSWER OF THE CREPC 1920 AD HOC COMMITTEE

        Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“FERC’s” or “Commission’s”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 the CREPC 1920 Ad Hoc

Committee2, on behalf of the NorthernGrid Relevant State Entities (“NorthernGrid RSEs”)3,

respectfully submits this Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer in response to the Motion

for Leave to Answer and Answer submitted by the NorthernGrid Enrolled Parties on August



1
  18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213 (2025).
2
  The CREPC 1920 Ad Hoc Committee was established by the Committee on Regional Electric Power
Cooperation’s Transmission Collaborative in order to facilitate the participation by the Relevant State Entities
in the NorthernGrid and WestConnect transmission planning regions’ State Engagement Periods and to
provide input into other aspects of the regions’ transmission providers’ FERC Order No. 1920 compliance
plans.
3
  The NorthernGrid RSEs participating in the CREPC 1920 Ad Hoc Committee include the California Energy
Commission, California Public Utilities Commission, Idaho Governor’s Office of Energy and Mineral
Resources, Idaho Public Utilities Commission, Montana Department of Environmental Quality, Montana
Public Service Commission, Oregon Department of Energy, Oregon Public Utility Commission, Public
Utilities Commission of Nevada, Utah Department of Commerce, Utah Office of Energy Development, Utah
Public Service Commission, Washington Department of Commerce, Washington Energy Facility Site
Evaluation Council, Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission, Washington State Office of the
Attorney General, Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality/Industrial Siting Council, Wyoming Energy
Authority, Wyoming Office of Consumer Advocate, and Wyoming Public Service Commission.



                                                                                                               1
 28, 2026 (“NorthernGrid Answer”)4 in the above-captioned proceedings. The NorthernGrid

Answer incorrectly characterizes as being unjust and unreasonable certain elements of the

NorthernGrid RSEs’ proposed ex ante cost allocation methodology.


I.      Motion for Leave to Answer


        Although Rule 213 prohibits most answers, FERC has permitted answers where

good cause exists, such as when the answer would produce a more complete record in the

proceeding5, lead to a better understanding of the issues6, permit the issues to be

narrowed or clarified7, or otherwise assist the Commission in its decision-making process.8

This CREPC 1920 Ad Hoc Committee Answer achieves each of these purposes.

        FERC Order No. 1920 establishes an unprecedented role for RSEs with regard to

regional transmission planning, including an opportunity for states to offer their own

proposed ex ante cost allocation methodology applicable to transmission projects

selected for development for purposes of cost allocation and to develop a State Agreement

Process (“SAP”) that enables states to attempt to reach agreement on an alternative to the

applicable ex ante methodology on a case-by-case basis. It is imperative, especially in this

instance, where the NorthernGrid Answer challenges the RSEs’ proposed ex ante cost

allocation methodology, that the NorthernGrid RSEs have an opportunity to enhance the




4
  Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of the Northern Grid Enrolled Parties (filed August 28, 2026)
(“NorthernGrid Answer”).
5
  See, e.g., Ohio Power Co., 46 FERC ¶ 61,180 at 61,595 (1989).
6
  See, e.g. Columbia Gas Transmission, LLC, 157 FERC ¶ 61, 247 at P 5 (2016).
7
  See, e.g. Southwest Power Pool, Inc., 135 FERC ¶ 61,223 at P 27 (2011).
8
  See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 182 FERC ¶ 61,073 at P 157 (2023).


                                                                                                        2
 Commission’s understanding of the failings associated with the objections the

NorthernGrid Enrolled Parties raise.


II.     Background


        Order No. 1920 required FERC-jurisdictional transmission providers in a planning

region to conduct a State Engagement Period with the RSEs in that region to, among other

things, enable the RSEs to provide input to the transmission providers as they developed a

proposed ex ante cost allocation methodology to be included in their Order No. 1920

compliance filings.9 The Commission also authorized the RSEs, if they wished, to develop

and propose a different ex ante cost allocation methodology.10 In addition, the RSEs were

provided the opportunity to develop and propose their own SAP, regardless of whether the

transmission providers in the region intended to include a SAP proposal in their compliance

filings.11 The transmission providers were required to attach the RSE cost allocation and

SAP proposals to their compliance filings as long as they received the state proposals by

the conclusion of the State Engagement Period.12 The Commission, recognizing the critical

role states play in the development of regionally planned transmission, included these

provisions in an effort to make the states more comfortable with the approach taken to




9
  Building for the Future Through Regional Electric Transmission Planning and Cost Allocation, Order No.
1920, 187 FERC ¶ 61,068 (2024) (Order No. 1920), order on reh’g and clarification, Order No. 1920-A, 189
FERC ¶ 61,126 (2024) (Order No. 1920-A), order on reh’g and clarification, Order No. 1920-B, 191 FERC ¶
61,026 (2025) (Order No. 1920-B).
10
   See Order No. 1920 at P 1359 and Order No. 1920-A at P 650.
11
   Order No. 1920 at P 1402; Order No. 1920-A at P 708.
12
   Order No. 1920-A at P 651.


                                                                                                           3
 potentially allocate regionally-planned transmission costs to the utilities they regulate and

the customers they are charged with protecting.13


            NorthernGrid hosted five State Engagement meetings with the RSEs. In addition,

the CREPC 1920 Ad Hoc Committee met 28 times to consider cost allocation and other

aspects of the regional transmission planning process required by Order No. 1920. Most of

those meetings were open to the public, including representatives of the NorthernGrid

Enrolled Parties.


            During the State Engagement Period the NorthernGrid RSEs determined that the

cost allocation methodology the Enrolled Transmission Providers intended to file with

FERC was insufficient. The RSEs concluded that a more creative approach is necessary to

address the unique characteristics of the West, where non-FERC jurisdictional utilities own

significant portions of the transmission grid but typically do not engage in regional

transmission planning as enrolled entities. This, in part, is the reason that neither

NorthernGrid nor WestConnect has selected and developed a single transmission project

pursuant to the Order No. 1000 regional transmission planning process.


            The NorthernGrid RSEs, in coordination with the WestConnect RSEs, developed

their own ex ante cost allocation proposal. This proposal contains three elements: (1) a

process that enables any regional entity to subscribe to capacity on transmission projects

selected for the purpose of cost allocation pursuant to the Order No. 1920 regional

planning process; (2) the allocation of a portion of project costs based on an analysis of



13
     Id. at P 659.


                                                                                             4
 project benefits and which Enrolled Parties (and their customers) will benefit; and (3) the

use of a solution-based distribution factor (“DFAX “) analysis to enhance confidence that

costs are being allocated in a manner roughly commensurate with benefits. The CREPC

1920 Ad Hoc Committee, on behalf of the NorthernGrid RSEs, submitted this proposal to

the NorthernGrid Enrolled Parties on April 28, 2026.


       The RSEs also that same day, through the CREPC 1920 Ad Hoc Committee,

submitted an RSE-developed SAP proposal to the NorthernGrid Enrolled Parties.

Subsequent discussions between representatives of the Enrolled Parties and the CREPC

1920 Ad Hoc Committee led to an agreed-upon version of an SAP that the Enrolled Parties

included in their Order No. 1920 compliance filings submitted to the Commission on June

12, 2026. This SAP proposal defines the circumstances under which the states would be

allowed to undertake development of a project-specific cost allocation alternative and how

the states would seek to reach agreement. If agreement is reached on an alternative cost

allocation method, the SAP outlines how the states’ agreed-upon proposal would be

forwarded to the Commission for review.


       In addition, the NorthernGrid RSEs on March 25, 2026, sent a letter to the

NorthernGrid Enrolled Parties offering comments on several non-cost allocation provisions

contained in a draft-version of the Enrolled Parties’ Order No. 1920 proposed tariff

amendments. Subsequently, the Enrolled Parties notified the RSEs that the final version of

the tariff amendments to be submitted in compliance with FERC Order No. 1920 addressed

the concerns raised by the RSEs except for a proposal by the RSEs that a new states

subcommittee be established to enhances the states’ role in the NorthernGrid


                                                                                              5
 transmission planning process. Discussions between NorthernGrid and the RSEs to

address this issue are ongoing.


        On June 12, 2026, each of the NorthernGrid Enrolled Parties submitted proposed

tariff amendments in compliance with FERC Order No. 1920.14 The compliance filings

included as attachments the RSEs’ ex ante cost allocation proposal. On August 5, 2026,

the CREPC 1920 Ad Hoc Committee and a group of public interest organization submitted

separate comments in response to the proposed tariff amendments and in support of the

NorthernGrid RSEs’ proposed ex ante cost allocation methodology. The Enrolled Parties on

August 28, 2026, filed a Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer in response to the August 5

comments.15


        The NorthernGrid Answer criticizes two elements of the RSEs’ proposed ex ante

methodology: (1) reliance on the solution-based DFAX analysis to determine in-part which

Enrolled Parties (and their customers) benefit from a proposed transmission project; and

(2) the RSEs’ proposal to except Enrolled Parties (and their customers) that are considered

to be receiving a de minimis level of benefits associated with a particular project from cost

allocation responsibility. The NorthernGrid Answer does not challenge any other aspect of

the RSEs’ ex ante cost allocation proposal. The CREPC 1920 Ad Hoc Committee seeks to

respond to the NorthernGrid Answer and its critique of the RSEs’ cost allocation proposal.



14
   See e.g., Order No. 1920 Compliance Filing of Nevada Power and Sierra Pacific Power Company Enrolled
Parties of NorthernGrid, Docket No. ER26-2818 (filed June 12, 2026).
15
   The public interest organized submitted a response to NorthernGrid Answer on September 14. Motion for
Leave to Answer and Answer of Renewable Northwest, Advanced Energy United, Interwest Energy Alliance,
Montana Environmental Information Center, Natural Resources Defense Council, NW Energy Coalition, and
Sustainable FERC Project.


                                                                                                           6
            FERC in Order No. 1920 and Order No. 1920-A established the State Engagement

Period and authorized the RSEs in a region to, if they choose, propose their own ex ante

cost allocation methodology and SAP. The Commission did so because it recognized that

states – both through their siting and general utility ratemaking authorities – can play a

significant role in ensuring that regionally planned transmission projects are actually

developed and that the benefits associated with those projects can be achieved. If states

are supportive of the cost allocation approach applicable to the transmission facility in

question, the Commission reasoned they may be more inclined to grant the regulatory

approvals necessary for transmission projects to proceed.16 It is therefore imperative that

FERC give deference to a just and reasonable RSE-proposed cost allocation approach that

differs from one proposed by a regional planning entity.


III.       Answer

           A. The RSEs’ Proposal Sufficiently Explains How the DFAX Analysis Would be
              Conducted


           It is well settled that the costs of transmission must be allocated in a manner

“roughly commensurate” with benefits.17 The RSEs proposed ex ante cost allocation

methodology relies upon three approaches to ensure that costs associated with a

transmission project selected for development for purposes of cost allocation pursuant to

a Long-Term Transmission Plan are appropriately allocated. First, transmission capacity

and associated costs would be allocated to entities through a subscription process run by



16
     Order No. 1920-A at P 659.
17
     Illinois Commerce Commission v. FERC, 721 F.3d 764 (7th Cir. 2013).


                                                                                              7
 the project developer. Second, for remaining capacity not acquired during the subscription

process, for transmission projects lower than 200 kV, 100% of the costs and capacity rights

would be allocated to the Enrolled Parties by assessing each of their proportionate shares

of total project benefits (based on the benefits identified in Order No. 192018). For

transmission projects between and inclusive of 200 kV and 300 kV, 90% of the remaining

costs would be allocated in this manner. For transmission projects over 300 kV, 75% of the

remaining costs would be allocated in this manner. Third, for those projects between and

inclusive of 200 kV and 300 kV and those projects exceeding 300 kV, 10% and 25% of the

remaining post-subscription process project capacity and costs, respectively, would be

allocated by utilizing a solution-based DFAX analysis to model the flow of power across the

new transmission project and the zones that are responsible for those flows.19


        The Enrolled Parties’ Answer argues that the tariff language proposed by the RSEs’

for their ex ante cost allocation proposal is “incomplete” because it does not establish the

zones in question.20 In addition, the Answer criticizes the RSEs’ proposal as not adequately

describing how the DFAX methodology would be employed.21


        Details focusing on how the solution-based DFAX method would be applied can be

included in a business practice manual. FERC’s “Rule of Reason” test establishes a three-

prong standard to determine whether an item must be addressed in a tariff provision as




18
   Order No. 1920-A at P 31.
19
   The RSEs’ proposed tariff language establishes that the Enrolled Parties would designate the zones to be
used for purposes of establishing beneficiaries pursuant to the solution-based DFAX methodology.
20
   NorthernGrid Answer at 5-6.
21
   Id. at 6.


                                                                                                              8
 opposed to a business practice manual: (1) whether the item will significantly affect rates,

terms, and conditions of FERC-jurisdictional service; (2) whether it establishes a rule that

can be drafted in a clear manner; and (3) whether the item can be understood as a

standard contractual provision or business practice.22


        A representative of NorthernGrid recently indicated to some RSE representatives

that NorthernGrid is contemplating developing a business practice manual. The details

associated with how the DFAX analysis will be implemented can and should be included in

that business practice manual. As Dr. Brooks’ affidavit notes, PJM already provides a

roadmap for how DFAX can be applied to cost allocation as it already partially relies on this

mechanism for Order No. 1000 cost allocation.23 Although a number of the details are

included in PJM’s tariff, there is no reason that those same details could not be adopted as

part of NorthernGrid’s business practice manual as a standard industry approach.


        Moreover, the RSEs’ ex ante cost allocation proposal explicitly provides for the

Enrolled Parties to designate the zones that will be used when the DFAX methodology is

applied. The Enrolled Parties are in a better position to determine the best approach for

dividing the NorthernGrid planning region into zones. As Dr. Brooks points out, it would not

be difficult for the Enrolled Parties to define the zones.24 The Enrolled Parties’ suggestion

that FERC is unable to assess whether the RSEs’ cost allocation approach is just and




22
   ISO New England, Inc., 187 FERC 61,100 (2024).
23
   Motion to Intervene and Comments of Renewable Northwest, Advanced Energy United, Interwest Energy
Alliance, Montana Environmental Information Center, Natural Resources Defense Council, NW Energy
Coalition, and Sustainable FERC Project (filed August 5, 2026) (“PIO Comments), Attachment A at 9-12.
24
    Id., Attachment A at 14.


                                                                                                        9
 reasonable without knowing exactly how the zones will be designated is non-sensical. The

Commission is equipped to make a judgement as to whether a requirement that the

Enrolled Parties designate the zones is sufficient to satisfy the requirements of the Federal

Power Act and Order No. 1920.


        Even if the Commission were to determine that the RSEs’ proposed ex ante cost

allocation tariff language requires further details, that is not a reason to reject the RSEs’

proposal. Unlike Federal Power Act Section 205 proceedings where the Commission

typically must accept or reject the entire tariff filing,25 FERC has latitude to respond to a

Section 206 compliance filing by accepting some provisions and directing that specific

revisions be made to the remaining items.26 The NorthernGrid RSEs are amenable to

offering additional details should the Commission require more information.


        B. Litigation Associated with PJM Cost Allocation Does Not Render DFAX
           Unjust and Unreasonable


        The NorthernGrid Answer points to several cases (both at FERC and on appeal)

where parties have challenged PJM’s transmission cost allocation methodology to infer that

the solution-based DFAX methodology is somehow unacceptable.27 The fact is that the

Commission has found that PJM’s use of the DFAX methodology as part of its regional

transmission cost allocation approach to be just and reasonable approach28 and has never



25
   NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108 (D.C. Cir. 2017).
26
   See e.g., New York Independent System Operator, Order on Compliance, 191 FERC ¶ 61,049 (2025). See
also Maryland Office of People’s Counsel v. FERC, No. 24-1353 (D.C. Cir. 2026).
27
   NorthernGrid Answer at 7.
28
   PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 142 FERC ¶ 61,214 (2013), order on reh’g and compliance, 147 FERC ¶ 61,128
(2014), order on reh’g and compliance, 150 FERC ¶ 61,038, and order on reh’g and compliance, 151 FERC ¶
61,250 (2015).


                                                                                                        10
 second-guessed that conclusion. In addition, no reviewing court has ever challenged this

conclusion.

          As Dr. Brooks points out in her affidavit the DFAX methodology actually helps

regional transmission planning entities determine both the level of benefits associated with

a new transmission project as well as the location of those benefits.29


          C. The Enrolled Parties Fail to Distinguish Alleged Infirmities Associated With
             DFAX From Their Own Cost Allocation Proposal


          The NorthernGrid Answer attempts to identify three additional concerns with the

RSEs’ proposed ex ante cost allocation methodology: (1) non-FERC jurisdictional utilities

would not (without volunteering to pay) be allocated costs even if the DFAX approach

demonstrates they will benefit; (2) the RSEs’ proposal does not take into account whether a

zone needs additional transmission capacity; and (3) DFAX depends on forecasted load

which is a concern because large loads may not materialize as expected in various zones. 30

What the Answer fails to point out is that these uncertainties also apply to the NorthernGrid

Enrolled Parties’ ex ante cost allocation proposal.




29
     PIO Comments, Attachment A at 13.
30
     NorthernGrid Answer at 8.


                                                                                            11
         The NorthernGrid Enrolled Parties’ proposed cost allocation methodology would

calculate the total value of the benefits FERC identified in Order No. 1000 and then

apportion project costs based on each Enrolled Party’s proportionate share of those

benefits. This approach suffers from the same types of uncertainties that NorthernGrid

alleges are a disqualifying problem with the RSEs’ DFAX methodology. First, non-

jurisdictional utilities may also benefit from a transmission project selected for

development as part of the NorthernGrid long-term regional transmission plan but those

benefits are to be ignored for the purposes of NorthernGrid’s cost allocation scheme.31

Second, the NorthernGrid Enrolled Parties’ proposal does not require a determination that

an Enrolled Party needs additional transmission capacity before the Enrolled Party can be

allocated costs. Finally, NorthernGrid’s long-term transmission planning process is equally

dependent on load forecasts. To the extent those forecasts suggest more transmission

capacity is needed and that transmission capacity is built, those costs would be assigned

to the Enrolled Parties. Regardless of the cost allocation methodology that will be

employed, regional transmission planners will need to have forecasts that are as accurate

as possible.




31
  This is one of the reasons the RSEs’ proposal is superior to NorthernGrid’s. Non-jurisdictional utilities can,
through the RSEs’ proposed subscription process, acquire capacity and, in turn, voluntarily pay for part of the
project’s costs.


                                                                                                             12
         D. The RSEs’ Proposed De Minimis Exception is Consistent with FERC
           Precedent and the “Roughly Commensurate” Standard


        The NorthernGrid Answer criticizes the RSEs’ proposal to except Enrolled

Transmission Providers from cost allocation responsibility if they are determined to be

receiving only a de minimis level of benefits.32 The RSEs’ proposal excepts Enrolled Parties

that would be assigned less than two percent of the allocated post-subscription costs from

cost responsibility. Instead, those costs would be reallocated to other Enrolled Parties that

are determined to be responsible for two percent or more of post subscription project

benefits. The Enrolled Parties argue that this approach raises cost causation concerns.


        FERC has previously approved the inclusion of a de minimis exception to PJM’s

transmission cost allocation methodology.33 Although FERC recently rescinded that

authorization,34 the Commission’s reasoning was based on the discriminatory nature with

which the PJM exception was applied, not because a de minimis exception is

impermissible.


        Both the courts and FERC have been clear – transmission cost allocation

mechanisms must ensure that project costs are allocated in a manner “roughly

commensurate with benefits”. That does not mean that a regional planning entity has to

with complete certainty ensure that each transmission provider pays no more and no less

than the exact amount it benefits. As the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit has



32
   NorthernGrid Answer at 9-10.
33
   PSEG Servs. Corp., Docket No. ER12-2412-000 (Sept. 19, 2012) (delegated order increasing the
applicability of the PJM de minimis exception).
34
   Consol. Edison Co. of New York, Inc. et al., 194 FERC ¶ 61,179 (2026).


                                                                                                  13
 noted: “We do not suggest that the Commission has to calculate benefits to the last

penny, or for that matter to the last million or ten million or perhaps hundred million

dollars.” Instead, the allocation of costs must be “roughly commensurate with benefits.”35

The RSEs’ understood that cost allocation is not an exact science and agreed that

NorthernGrid Enrolled Parties and their customers should not be forced to pay for a

transmission project from which they do not significantly benefit if they benefit at all.36


IV.     Conclusion


        For these reasons, the 1920 Ad Hoc Committee respectfully requests that the

Commission accept this Answer and approve the NorthernGrid RSEs’ proposed ex ante

cost allocation methodology.

        Dated October 1, 2026




35
  ICC v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470 at 477 (7th Cir. 2009).
36
  The NorthernGrid Enrolled parties suggest that the RSEs’ proposed de minimis exception conflicts with
another provision in the RSEs’ ex ante cost allocation proposal that requires that, if NorthernGrid were to
undertake portfolio planning an Enrolled Party should not be assigned costs in excess of what the Enrolled
Party would assigned had the multiple selected projects been selected separately. RSEs do not agree that
such a conflict exists (because the de minimis exception would apply equally under either planning
approach) but, nonetheless, the NorthernGrid Answer’s point is moot since the NorthernGrid Enrolled
Parties, did not, in their compliance filings, propose they would engage in portfolio planning.
